title: Nicole Quinn | Investing in Today's Popular Culture | Talks at Google
description:
Author Nicole Quinn discusses her career as a consumer investor and the importance of investing and supporting the female founder community, ensuring that underestimated founders are represented across technology.

For more information on Nicole, please visit https://lsvp.com/team-member/nicole-quinn/. 

Nicole is a General Partner at Lightspeed Venture Partners, where she focuses on Consumer, FinTech and Health investing. Consumer behavior, founder insights, and company brand are core in Nicole’s mind. She is on the board of beehiiv, Lightyear, Multiverse, Calm, Daybreak, Goop, Cameo and Lady Gaga's Haus Labs. Earlier, she sourced Rothy's and Zola. She has an MBA from Stanford and was on The Forbes Midas Brink List.

Moderated by Michael Carney.
summary: Nicole Quinn argues that the investment landscape is defined by broad consumer trends spanning fintech, AI, SaaS, health, and e-commerce, with a specific emphasis on mental health and substance abuse solutions as the next major tailwind. She advocates for the universal adoption of newsletters as a tool for individuals and teams to build direct customer relationships and monetize content through advertising matches, citing beehiiv as a platform that enables this model without requiring customers to pay.

transcript: MICHAEL CARNEY: Hello, and welcome, everyone. Welcome to this special Talks at Google virtual event. My name is Michael Carney, and I am so excited to introduce today's guest, Nicole Quinn. For background on Nicole-- and Nicole is a general partner at Lightspeed Venture Partners, where she focuses on consumer fintech and health investing. Consumer behavior, founder insights, and company brand are core in Nicole's mind. She's currently on the board of beehiiv, Lightyear, Multiverse, Calm, Daybreak, Goop, Cameo, and Lady Gaga's HAUS Labs. Earlier, she sourced Rothy's and Zola. She is currently an MBA from Stanford and was on the Forbes Midas Brink list. Lastly, quick disclosure that none of the following should be taken as investment advice from Nicole. Nicole, it is my absolute pleasure to welcome you on stage to Talks at Google. And thanks so much for joining us today. NICOLE QUINN: Thanks so much for having me, Michael. MICHAEL CARNEY: Absolutely. And for everyone, too, that's watching, please feel free to drop questions into the chat. We'll get to those throughout the session. But, Nicole, I'd love to just kick things off, if you could just tell us about yourself, your backstory of how you arrived at Lightspeed, where you're at today, and just how you arrived here. NICOLE QUINN: Yes, of course, will do. So first of all, thank you very much for having me. And you can tell by the very odd accent that I originally grew up in England, but I have an Australian dad and I've been here for 10 years. So I think my accent's all over the place. But I had an entrepreneurial dad, which is probably where I got my love and thirst for entrepreneurship and startups. And so back in the 1990s, he was building online marketplaces, mainly pharmacies around the UK and continental Europe. And I mainly learned lessons on what not to do. I actually think you learn more in life from things that don't go as planned. And so I definitely learned a lot of lessons sort of pre-2000 crash on what not to do in tech startups. So I studied maths. I went into finance, again, pre-financial crash. So it was an exciting thing to go to at that point. But I spent nearly a decade there, between London and New York, equity research most of the time. I got to do the Facebook group on Pandora IPOs. So I really started to love big tech, I would say. But at that point, a lot of those companies were just a fraction of where they are today. And so it was really working with them from two years before their IPO right through to their IPO on, hey, how has Facebook become the brand name that it is today-- the same for Google? And that really, again, got me loving this world. So I went to a fintech startup, did angel investing, and then actually came out to Stanford to do an MBA, and I feel like, like most people who do MBAs, started my own startup. And I actually pitched it to most of the VCs on Sand Hill Road. And that was how I met Lightspeed. So it was really terrific to be able to see Lightspeed from the other side of the table as a founder and to be able to think, OK, well, what kind of partner will they really be? And to me, I felt like Lightspeed would never be a passive investor. They would really help me. They would roll up their sleeves. They would do the work. It's a little bit like going to the gym, right? If you have a growth mindset, you kind of want your muscles to be broken down and built up stronger by going to the gym. And this is like the investment version of that. And so I love the partners there. I felt like they made me better, and so worked with them for a couple of years during business school and then joined as a VC afterwards. And that was, gosh, about eight years ago now. MICHAEL CARNEY: Wow. Oh, my gosh. Well, thank you for walking us through from end to end your whole experience. I'm curious towards your current days at Lightspeed and first, just what excites you the most about investing today, investing at Lightspeed today? To your point around when you first were introduced to the ecosystem, what's really exciting in today's world in your day? NICOLE QUINN: So I co-head our consumer investing group, and so I definitely do a lot of consumer. But I always say it's consumer in the broadest sense of the word. And so that means everything from consumer fintech to consumer and prosumer AI, consumer SaaS products, definitely consumer health, as well as all your typical e-commerce, marketplaces, social. And so where I'm spending the bulk of my time today is definitely AI-- let's come on to that in more detail later-- mental health, on the board of three mental health companies, and just thinking about-- there's been so many tailwinds for really terrific mental health solutions over the past five years. And so what is the next tailwind area like that? Maybe it's substance abuse help and marketplaces to really provide those solutions. Maybe it's more help for adolescents-- and so excited to talk about some of the companies on the mental health side of things, as well as AI. And great companies like beehiiv-- beehiiv, if you guys don't know, is-- think of Mailchimp and Klaviyo but for you, really for this generation. And so it is an incredible platform for you to build a newsletter. So my belief is that everybody should have a newsletter. I have one. Lightspeed has one. Google should have one more broadly, but it also should be for every team and for every individual. And beehiiv makes it so simple to go on, to start your newsletter, and then to be able to really understand your customer, be able to do the surveys and really understand in granular detail who your customer is. And then what the magic is, is that you don't have to then charge your customer. You can if you want to. You can do a subscription. But the better thing is they'll be like, OK, Michael loves golf. He's going to have a golf newsletter. And so they'll match you with folks who want to advertise on a golf newsletter. And so you will get paid to write your golf newsletter. The customers don't have to pay, and they'll just match you with the right advertiser. And it's growing incredibly quickly. So that's a really cool one and some of the areas we love to invest in at the moment. MICHAEL CARNEY: I'm so excited and happy you mentioned beehiiv because-- fun fact-- I have my own newsletter through beehiiv currently. So I can speak to just my experience just writing and the amazing community and just how awesome the community has been as I've kind of dove into deep end of writing for the first time ever and kind of putting all my experience down on paper. And I've even gone through beehiiv's courses and so on. And so I also follow your newsletter quite a bit if you want to give a quick plug to you and Faraz's newsletter, which I know you share quite regularly, too, through beehiiv. NICOLE QUINN: We did not know this about each other. So I did not even set you up for that. That is really great you have a beehiiv newsletter. I truly believe everybody should. First of all, send me yours because I want to see it. And, yes, ours is called "Buzzworthy." So straight after investing in beehiiv, which is B-E-E-H-I-I-V-- really cool spelling, kind of similar to Google, right? It's sort of, hey, you're just going to create your own name. And so that's exactly what beehiiv have done, and it's an incredible product. So, yeah, follow me on beehiiv "Buzzworthy." MICHAEL CARNEY: Definitely. I will send you mine afterwards, would love any feedback. My newsletter or just my subscriptions, too, have been growing, which has been fun to see. I think you bring up a great area we can move into as well as just around mental health. Sneak preview-- my next post will be around mental health and just navigating that, especially through the holidays. But you mentioned mental health quite a bit. And I guess my first question for you, just knowing the companies that you've invested in and where you currently sit on the boards of, which we can cover in a second here, but how do you think technology can be really used today to just improve mental health care in that whole area? NICOLE QUINN: So it's interesting. I feel like, if you think about it, 5, 10, years ago, we just did not think about mental health in the same way. Especially me growing up in England, it was very much like, keep calm and carry on. Never talk about your problems. And that has really changed. I never even understood the word "anxiety" growing up in England. Nobody talked about it, but everybody had it. And so first of all, it has been the tailwinds of all of that changing. And then the technology-- well, where Lightspeed loves to invest is where there's a technology overlay on an existing human behavior. And so to give a non-mental health one, when we invested in Snapchat, people have been taking cheeky photos and then the next day waking up and thinking, oh, my gosh I wish that that was deleted. And so enter Snapchat. And it really is exactly that where we love to invest. And so Calm, for example-- folks had been reading children bedtime stories to help them fall asleep. It is proven that bedtime stories help you get to sleep. And so having the technology overlay of someone like Stephen Fry reading to you about the lavender fields in Provence-- which is, by the way, how I get to sleep every night-- is really powerful. And it is just so helpful to be able to go to sleep without drugs, just by your favorite person talking to you about your favorite place. It's really relaxing. And so the same thing for Real-- we realized that the demand in this country for therapists is so high, and it's just not scalable to think about the number of therapists. They're just not going to be able to meet that demand. And so Real offers a much more scalable solution. So it's like saying, hey, listen. If you're an alcoholic, you go to Alcoholics Anonymous because it's clinically proven that group therapy works for people who are or have been an alcoholic. And so why not apply that same thinking to anxiety, depression, anger? It really helps folks to understand that, hey, you had anger, and how did you deal with it, and how does it manifest itself? OK, that makes me feel understood and heard. I think one of the most basic cravings that we have as a human being is to feel heard and understood. I tell my husband this every day. And so it really is something that Real can dramatically help with. I hope that Google offers Real at some point and would really encourage any HR benefit folks listening to offer Real because it is a lower price point. It is a much more scalable solution but clinically proven to reach the same results, if not better. And then the last one that I really want to talk about is through investing in these other companies, I realized that the most important thing is that we are targeting adults. But these mental health issues, complications, they start at a much younger age. They start at three, four, five. 90% of the brain development happens before you're five years old. And so it really is thinking about, hey, what kind of mental health solutions can be offered to children, to teenagers? And so that's why we invested in Daybreak, which is offering schools right now, but we will definitely expand the platform, to offer therapy and then, again, scalable solutions to younger folks. And I think that is so important. I now have children that are only three and one. But I'm constantly thinking about the mental health solutions that, quite frankly, everybody in this country needs, to some extent and at some point in their life. So it's really special to live in this day and age when we have those solutions through technology. MICHAEL CARNEY: I love what you just covered there. And shoutout-- you mentioned Calm, Real, and Daybreak Health. I have to also give a huge shout out to Real. Especially during the pandemic, Real was an app I was on heavily throughout that period, and being comfortable sharing that, being vulnerable, and sharing that, too, with others. And then I use Calm daily to just-- I use it also for gratitude notes and what I'm thankful for and just how I'm feeling as sort of a check-in and a light check-in throughout the day as well. And I couldn't agree more with just hearing your describing what mental-- what some of the challenges mental health companies are trying to solve for. You shared a bit, too, about investing in mental health startups. But any advice to founders, too, who are currently building in this space, too, as we move forward? And we're going through the holidays now. We're getting ready for the New Year. Is there anything to that that's top of mind for you as we close out the year related to mental health? NICOLE QUINN: So first of all, you know all the cool products I love it. MICHAEL CARNEY: Yes. NICOLE QUINN: I need to actually got a list from you after this of all the products that you actually use outside our portfolio because we probably should be looking at investing in those, after this. MICHAEL CARNEY: Totally. NICOLE QUINN: So if I was building in this space right now, I really would think about how AI can help not just mental health, but across the board in health. So I think our hopes and wishes for AI impacting health care are quite far off. I feel like they have not really hit today in the same dramatic way that they've helped, say, prosumer companies, right? And so if you look at Notion, they're already doing a significant amount of revenue through their AI product that they've built within Notion, and similar other companies like that. But it's like, what does that look like for health? And so for me, I think about what AI can really do in terms of giving you the ability to understand what loved ones are going through and really help you be able to create content and go through that data and be able to know if one of your friends is having a tough time. I mean, we have a huge friend graph. And one of my friends from growing up actually committed suicide last weekend. And-- MICHAEL CARNEY: Oh, my god. NICOLE QUINN: Now hundreds of friends get together, and it's like, god, why didn't we do that before? It's because we didn't know. And I really think that is where technology is able to show folks, hey, this friend of yours, they need your help right now. They're really struggling. These are the things that they're googling, and they really need your help. And so I would love for folks to be able to have a smaller close-knit group where we're saying to one another, are you OK? How are people doing that day? Like a traffic light system, for example-- and so thinking about how, as a community, we can really help one another from a mental health position, but then also other areas outside mental health. I talked about substance abuse. And there's some really interesting marketplaces there helping with opioid addiction. Then we've invested in an interesting company around the posttraumatic stress disorder space. And that is a really interesting area, again, where AI can help. But for me, I think we've just like touched the tip of the iceberg with how AI can help in health care, and not just thinking about as consumer health care, but whether it sells to companies, whether it sells to schools, payers, consumers, just putting it all together and thinking about what are the best solutions there. And those are the ones that we really need to be starting as a founder. I hope that if you have any ideas in this space, I really hope that you think-- this picture behind me says "Dream big dreams." MICHAEL CARNEY: Yeah. NICOLE QUINN: And so I really hope that you think, hey, listen, if my idea that I could be the biggest it could possibly be, what would that look like, and then go out there and build it. And there's definitely investors like myself that really want to invest in companies like that. MICHAEL CARNEY: Well, so sorry for your loss, and thank you for being vulnerable and sharing. know I want to speak for our viewers, and just our condolences to you, too, as we close out the year and so on. I can't even imagine, Nicole, losing someone-- NICOLE QUINN: And I think these-- MICHAEL CARNEY: --so close like that. NICOLE QUINN: --are the toughest times of the year, you know? Around the holidays is unfortunately the time where there are the highest rates of suicide, et cetera. And so we more than ever need to be there for friends and family around this time of year. MICHAEL CARNEY: I love that. I think there couldn't be a better time to be hosting this talk and having this conversation, too, around mental health. It worked out perfectly, just as you mentioned. So many times, you feel like you're running towards the holidays. And often now it's like you're running away, just because of everything that might be going on. There's no easy way to transition. But something you mentioned, too, was just also talking about marketplaces. And you've had some really great thoughts and just put out a lot of amazing words of wisdom out in the community about marketplaces in that particular area-- just taking a step back of what has been your experience just investing in marketplaces, and how has that evolved, too, over time? You mentioned AI a little bit, but just curious your point of view there. NICOLE QUINN: So Lightspeed has been investing, gosh, for a decade or more in incredible marketplaces, like Grubhub on the consumer side, like Faire on the SMB side, really helping all the many, many small shops and boutiques in this country to be able to source the very best products. Max Rhodes from Faire is an exceptional founder who actually built the Square Cash Pay app within Square. And so when we met him really early on, we're like, wow, this is somebody who's very, very strong. And so my partner, Alex Taussig, I think he is the best marketplace investor on the Street. And he creates such terrific content. I need to get him to move across to beehiiv. His newsletter is called "Drinking from the Fire Hose," and I highly recommend. Actually, for anybody with any kind of entrepreneurial thoughts, he goes through such detailed analysis of what investors want to see with different marketplaces at different stages of the business, how to think about the strength of a marketplace. We love to do cohort analysis. And so it's like, OK, listen. Typically, your very early cohorts are going to be your strongest because they're going to be your friends and family who are buying from you. And then the cohorts will typically get a little bit worse. Maybe people are doing smaller average ticket items or purchases. Or they may be buying a little bit more infrequently. But then what we want to see is that the cohort start to get better and better as people say, wow, this is a marketplace that I absolutely love and trust and I want to come back to time and time again. And so for me, gosh, you know, I think I started on Instacart with, like, one a month, and now I'm on there, like, every two days, which is, again, a factor of having kids. They always need extra little things. I'm so grateful for that marketplace. And they've done some pretty special things. Sometimes I think introducing a subscription as part of that marketplace is very smart for a particular business. And so for Instacart saying, OK, no delivery fees-- you've got to pay $100 a year, but then no delivery fees, well, that's really smart. Same with DoorDash. And so it just captures me in there. And I think, well, why would I even go down to the supermarket? Because I'm not even paying a delivery fee, even though they do mark up, like, 100% on chicken, for example, and 50% on bananas. But you don't think about that because you're getting free delivery. So we like to be very analytical around the marketplaces that we invest in and, yeah, highly recommend Alex Taussig's "Drinking from a Fire Hose." MICHAEL CARNEY: So many great recommendations and companies to follow. So you mentioned-- we talked about mental health, giving an example, too, of Instacart. But also, just double-clicking a little bit into that, how do you think marketplaces in particular can be used to just disrupt the existing technologies and existing sectors there, too? NICOLE QUINN: I would say across the board. I mean, even as you think about a lot of these mental health solutions, a lot of them were marketplaces that helped with therapists. And so there's no need for the companies to have 1099 employees. Instead, it makes much more sense for it to be like a marketplace and connecting us to therapists. And then one of the big unlocks for Headway, for example, was really when they allowed insurance. Instead of me having to pay $200 to see a therapist, OK, great. Well, 95% gets covered by the payer. And so I only have to pay $10 a session. That is a really powerful model. And so, yeah, we do kind think about two-sided or three-sided marketplaces. With Faire, for example, it is the boutique and the brand and the customer. And so we've got to think about that. And that's also why marketplaces are so difficult to build in the early days. It is capital-intensive. That's why VC dollars are so important in marketplaces, because you compare it to e-commerce, for example. E-commerce, you could take maybe $1, $2 million, or no capital ever, and you could really build a massive e-commerce business that is also profitable. Marketplaces, that's near to impossible. It would take a really long time. And so you do need a lot of that VC investment up front. And over time, your cap does decrease in marketplaces as opposed to e-commerce, where, typically, the cap increases over time, or consumer subscriptions, where it sort of stays flat and slightly increases. But marketplaces, it does decrease because of that word of mouth because of the way that it grows so virally. We love the network effects that are associated with marketplaces. So those are some of the areas, I would say-- and mental health and food delivery in the retail business like Faire that we get really excited about, and even Zola, for example, what happened during the pandemic, when everybody suddenly stopped doing weddings, and they were not using Zola during that time, well, Zola had built an incredible marketplace for their household goods. And so people just started shopping there. And that is what really helped that business to grow. And now we're back to having weddings again. So great-- you've got the wedding marketplace and the homeware marketplace. And so, yeah, we're on the board of that company and really love it. MICHAEL CARNEY: The amount of weddings that-- invitations that came through and just after the pandemic and so on is just-- I think of Zola so much because of just, yeah, how many weddings I have to attend and traveling to these days. And you totally read my mind. I was going to ask your thoughts about the network effects and how that affects marketplaces. But you just described it perfectly across some of those examples with Faire and Zola and how that really just leads to exponential growth through network effects, essentially. NICOLE QUINN: By the way, you're getting a lot of wedding invites because people are-- because you've got a lot of friends, Michael. That's exactly why [INAUDIBLE] getting so many wedding invites. MICHAEL CARNEY: It's true. It's true. It's a good problem to have, right, and just trying to manage the calendar these days and so on. Speaking a bit, too, you mentioned Snapchat earlier as well. And I think it's such a great tie-in to the mental health aspect as well. And we're chatting a bit about something that's been so much on top of everyone's mind-- social media and so on, and how does that maybe affect mental health? And just a bit of a broader question-- what are your thoughts on just the future of social media moving forward and, yeah, and how it's impacted your own thoughts and investing, even, too? NICOLE QUINN: Yeah, of course. So social is really interesting. And we have done a lot of analysis at Lightspeed on the social space. So social really goes in waves. And so you have, well, pretty much everything, I would say, in technology really goes in waves, right? And so you have the internet boom. Then you have the one around mobile. And we're going to talk about that in a second with regards to social. And now you have AI, which we'll come back to. So between the years of, like, 2007 and 2012, during that mobile wave, when you really saw the App Store be developed and so many different apps pop up, and people didn't have, necessarily, at that point, all of their different home screen apps. Now we have our home screen apps. We know what's there. It's so hard to have home screen displacement, as we like to call it. It's like, listen, if you're kind of using your Gmail app and your Google Calendar, Google Maps-- you guys are my entire bottom row. MICHAEL CARNEY: Oh, gosh. Good to know. Good to know. NICOLE QUINN: Then it's so difficult for that to be displaced. In fact, COVID was a time where that was because suddenly, you're moving Uber off your home screen app. You're moving Lyft off because you're not really taking those anywhere. And so there was an opportunity for new ones to come on. And that was why apps like Clubhouse, apps like BeReal, suddenly were not just being used but right there on your home screen app every single day. And so I often think, out of sight, out of mind. If you're not looking at it every day, you're not going to use it every day. But people were seeing it every day on their home screen app. And they were thinking, I'm kind of bored at home. I've got more time. So I'm going to go on to Clubhouse. And we just saw such a meteoric rise during COVID. But unfortunately, it didn't have the staying power. Now, what is different now/even during COVID versus that wave? Well, again, during that wave of 2007-2012, there are not those other opportunities. And so the social media apps took away from other areas. So we only have a certain number of hours in our day. So where does the social media app come from? Well, it actually took the place of cable television. And so the unbundling of cable television-- people would spend on average about $100 a year on cable. Well, we're taking that out, and that gives us $100 a year in extra disposable income to spend on $10 for Calm, $10 for Netflix, $10 for Apple Television, and then far more of these other apps that we really do have the money to spend on and the time to spend on it, most importantly. But then, during COVID, there was nothing that that time was coming from. That time was coming from maybe commute time, maybe the fact you weren't seeing your friends. And so as soon as we went back to seeing people in real life, well, you just didn't necessarily need Clubhouse anymore. And do you need BeReal? Well, it's fun. It's cool. But, hey, I've been using Snapchat for the last seven years. I'm going to go back to using Snapchat. And so that's why social has been so difficult over the last few years and why we haven't invested as much in social. But-- that's a big but-- I think now it's different. Now it's different because of this AI wave. I think that this new technology really is creating new opportunities for products that are so superior to what we previously had just on mobile. And so that's why you're seeing not just OpenAI, ChatGPT, but also Character, for example. Character.AI, to me, is like the future of fun, the future of entertainment. And people are taking away from other areas to spend their time and their hard-earned money, to some extent-- I'm sure they'll monetize more in the future. But right now, it's pretty much a free, incredible platform that folks can go on to and talk to any character that they want through AI. And so for me, that is a version of social. There's other really cool social apps that we've been looking at, like Can of Soup, for example, which we'll say, OK, let's do Michael in the most crazy Halloween outfit. [LAUGHTER] Look at yourself in all these different Halloween outfits. It's just AI-generated really amazing images. So I think you can tell I can talk on this subject for a long time. But, yes, the AI wave is going to be dramatically different for social and pretty much every sector. MICHAEL CARNEY: It's everywhere, right? And, well, first, I know our community and Googlers will absolutely love that you have so many Google products on your home screen there, as you mentioned, the calendar, Gmail. Maybe another time when we chat. We'll just see how much more we'll continue to take up space on Nicole's home screen. NICOLE QUINN: Oh, I have more-- Nest, Ring. MICHAEL CARNEY: Oh, my gosh. Yeah, you are-- yes, you are, hands down, becoming a favorite of our Talks guests and so on. Also, I know you mentioned with the mobile side of things, I recently started using Yaysay, which is another Lightspeed portfolio company. And even I've noticed-- I try to be the best son in the world and shop for my mom with some of the discounts and stuff. And she's like, I'm getting all these amazing deliveries from Yaysay? What is this company that you've been ordering from? But there's a really cool social component where you can kind of see other shoppers that are sharing on the app and seeing discounts and stuff coming through. And I'm trying to be the best son in the world, Nicole, and trying to spoil my mom through getting ready for the holidays. So-- NICOLE QUINN: I think you're winning. I think you are the best son in the world, Michael. I like it. MICHAEL CARNEY: I'm trying to get there. NICOLE QUINN: Good plug for you, isn't it? MICHAEL CARNEY: We're getting closer. Yes, yes, a great plug. And you've written so much, too, about social, and then you mentioned products and brands. I'm curious your perspective, too, on what will the impact of social be kind of on brands moving forward, on those companies and how they see maybe even social? NICOLE QUINN: So Yaysay is a really great example, actually. And so let's come back to that in just a second because it's interesting. As we think about physical products, there was obviously that huge wave of D2C or DNVBs, Digitally Native Vertical Brands. I guess-- what years was that? That was, like, 2016 to 2020, I would say. And all of those direct-to-consumer brands were essentially treated on tech multiples. And we invested in companies like Rothy's when they just had, like, a million in revenue. And what was fascinating was they did, like, $2 million in their first year, 30 their second year, 100 their third year, 300 their fourth year. And so even if-- whether you're treated on a tech multiple or not, some of those companies just really reach significant scale because they were just loved products. And they really had done an incredible job of hitting, I would say millennials and Gen Zs, on the values that they really cared about. Why would we need to wear any other shoe when we can wear a plastic recycled bottle that is really helping the environment, but also one that is incredibly comfortable? It's like a hug for your foot. It's like wearing a sock on your foot. And so then, when they went into other materials and bags, it was great because it really kind of worked for folks's values. And that was a big thing, I would say, in terms of the physical products back then. Then we needed to think about, OK, well all of the different social products, Instagram, et cetera, changed everything for these brands because it really meant that they were able to find scalable, repeatable marketing channels. And that, to us, is so key in any kind of product. And listen, yes, you could advertise on Pinterest, but maybe there's sort of a ceiling, whereas Instagram, Facebook, you can spend many, many millions. I have companies that spend $200 million a year advertising on Facebook/Instagram-- the same with Google. The ceiling is so high. And so they then found these scalable, repeatable marketing channels. They could build these businesses into multibillion-dollar businesses. And there were exits, like the Dollar Shave Clubs and the Jetts of the world. And so social dramatically helped. But the issue is that the algorithm on Facebook changed, all the iOS 14 changes on the data side of things. And so suddenly, it was much more expensive to acquire a customer. The unit economics didn't work so well. And so we're now constantly thinking about, what are the new channels that these products can grow? Yaysay is a really great one, which marries social and discounts together everything that customers love into just a really fun user experience. I highly recommend it-- Yaysay, Y-A-W and then S-A-W-- sorry-- Y-A-Y-S-A-Y. MICHAEL CARNEY: [INAUDIBLE] NICOLE QUINN: And it's just a really cool product. And then I would just say, yeah, that's exactly the kind of direction that people are going. It's like, hey, influencers, maybe that could be a scalable, repeatable marketing channel. And so we need to be thinking about whether it's your friends recommending or influencers recommending or getting discounts through Yaysay but also seeing what your friends/community are buying. That's a big direction that I think physical products-- the world is moving. MICHAEL CARNEY: Incredible. Well, I know we only have a bit more time left, and there's so much more we could cover. And we've got some great questions that are coming also through into the chat. I guess to maybe close us out a little bit around AI, as you mentioned, and talking so much there, you covered a bit already. But do you have any thoughts, too, on just the future of consumer and AI as we move into these next few years where it feels like AI is just going to continue to be at the forefront of everything in our world? NICOLE QUINN: Yes. So I think, on the prosumer side, wildly excited because we've invested in a company called Tome, T-O-M-E. And for me, I don't know why anybody builds a deck or any kind of digital product like that on anything other than Tome now. It's just such a great user experience. And the AI just means you can do it in, like, half the time. And so like pulling up, like, what does this mean-- well, AI essentially is just making everything we do a little bit easier, a little bit faster. And so if I'm sitting down to write my beehiiv newsletter, before ChatGPT and the world of generative AI really took off, it might have taken me, like, 5 to 10 hours to write that. Now I can get that written in a couple of hours. And so, wow, I'm getting 3 to 8 hours back in my day? Well, that's pretty special. And so it's almost like a customer has woken up and won the lottery of time because they now can actually make money through those other areas. But they're being able to do them faster, and they're getting time back in their day. So you're getting more money, and you're getting more time. And so it's like, what do you do with that? Well, they then think that we will spend it-- spend that extra time on new interesting areas. So I think we'll spend it on social-- hence my bullishness around social AI. I think we will spend that on more travel, more experiences. I would say some of the travel marketplaces like Expedia have tried to add an AI offering, but it's pretty limited now to an AI version of customer support. But if we really think big, what could that look like? Well, that actually could be huge in terms of the travel itineraries and understanding the very best travel experience. And instead of spending, like, 50 hours planning a trip, it can be done for you, and you're spending, like, an hour just reviewing the data and information. And so we're wildly excited about what AI does, yes, for fintech. Enterprise, I would say, we're investing in significantly right now. I'm not sure whether folks saw the information this morning on Biden's executive order just essentially injecting a degree of certainty into the debate around the guardrails for AI. And what this just means is that there is going to be more government oversight around advanced AI projects. And so we, as a result, will probably be investing far more so in AI security and that whole world. And so at Lightspeed, we've invested in 53 companies over a billion dollars in AI. MICHAEL CARNEY: Wow. NICOLE QUINN: And you should certainly expect that to continue. That wasn't all just this year. We definitely invested before the generative AI world. But for us, we're going to be significantly investing because we just think that whether it be on the enterprise side, security, prosumer, health, fintech, consumer, that whole space, it's changing the landscape. MICHAEL CARNEY: Completely. I also feel like I just got some great writing tips on how you go about shaving, like, 10 hours of writing into, like, maybe 5 or even, like, a third of that now. So thank you because that's been a bit of a challenge just figuring out how-- where is the time to be able to write and put down some deeper thoughts? I couldn't agree more with Tome. I love Tome. I use Tome regularly now, too. When I'm creating invites, even recording and giving a little bit of a speak over on an invite page, too, Tome just been so, so incredible. For the sake of time, just because we do have a few questions, too, but I also just wanted to also focus a bit on your amazing support within the female founder community and all the amazing work you've done. I listed off a few portfolio companies, too, that are female founder-led and just want to recognize that and just get your thoughts, too, on-- can you speak a little bit more about your work? And then are there any resources you recommend for female founders, too, that they can utilize and so on and just things that you follow and lean in with? NICOLE QUINN: This is such an important topic for me. I strongly believe that the best decisions get made when you have diversity around the table. And, yes, that's diversity of gender, but it's also diversity of opinions, experience, background, socioeconomic. And so for us, that is what is so key. And that's the best decisions around a VC table, the best decisions at a boardroom table, any kind of a Google decision-making table. And so what does that mean? What does that mean? We have to make these changes. Well, for us at Lightspeed, it's like, don't try and make changes externally before you do it internally. And now more than a third of our investors are women. We have 11 incredible female investors just in the US and Europe, more in India and China and Israel. And so for us, we've made those changes. And then we've made a lot of really terrific changes internally around everything for the working mother to making sure they're really supported. But then, for our portfolio companies, what we were doing is we asked them to sign a letter. And we said in this letter, you commit to, for every board member or senior hire that you make, you consider all underrepresented minorities. And so then signing this means that they're not going to say, oh, you know, I played golf with this guy, and I want to bring him in, which generally results in you hiring a person like yourself and all these sort of unconscious biases that we have. And so as a result of consciously saying, I will consider all underrepresented minorities, you are going to make sure that the pipeline is so much stronger and the very best candidate gets the job. And so those are some of the things that we've done both at Lightspeed but also for our 800 portfolio companies. And it is really important. And then with regards to your question around advice for female founders, the only advice that I would say that's separate to female founders is, again, this idea around think really big because one change that we noticed is that when guys give their projections for the three-year plan of what their startup's going to do, typically, they don't hit those numbers. And VCs know they're not going to hit those numbers. And so you have to discount them, like, 30% a year. But that's still great because they've kind of said to you they're going to grow, like, 10x a year, whereas the female founders-- and also, by the way, it's also geography as well. I find European founders, this is true of as well-- will be much more conservative and will say we believe we're going to grow 2.5X a year. And then they consistently come in above that, growing 3X, 3 and 1/2 X a year. And so I would just say think big because sometimes VCs are going to discount those projections when we build our own model. So we just want you to say, hey, if everything goes right, how big can this possibly be? And what does that mean for this idea I have for this business I'm building? How big an opportunity could it be? And so that is really the advice that I would give for female founders. And we're really starting to see that. I actually have noticed a huge change in that even just in the last few years, which has been terrific to see. I'm so excited to see more of that. MICHAEL CARNEY: That's incredible. I know we're almost at time. We have a great question, too. You've been on such an incredible journey since joining Lightspeed and investing in the female founder community, supporting mental health companies, consumer-led brands and companies as well with the focus on AI. We get a question a lot oftentimes. This one's from Simone, but any advice for folks who are just new to investing? What are some of the things we should keep top of mind as we start up ourselves, as maybe even individuals? NICOLE QUINN: I am so glad you asked this question. Folks usually say to me, like, how do I get into VC? And my answer to that is act like you're a VC before you're a VC. And what that means in practice is exactly this question, which is, OK, so even if you don't want to go into VC, investing on the side is a great idea because if you live in Silicon Valley or any other of the great hubs that are producing these incredible companies, and if you're at Google and you're able to say, oh, I worked with Noam, and now he started Character.AI, I had the opportunity to be able to invest in him or any other folks at Google, my gosh, take that opportunity. So I would say advice that I would have is definitely invest. Definitely do some angel investing. Maybe bring together an angel investing syndicate. And so investing whatever it may be, 25K, 50K, but then maybe putting together a Google syndicate-- I think that some folks from Twitter did this. And they called it #angels. And so it'd be cool to see the same in terms of a Google angel syndicate because when you come together as a group, you can then say, OK, great. Now we're going to invest, say, 500K between the 10 of us. And then we'd love to make an impact in this business and have a real voice at the table. And so we'd love to see you guys doing more in terms of angel syndicates. And then maybe someone can blog about what they're doing. Again, this could be, like, Google Angels beehiiv newsletter, where we started off, and then talk about the companies you invested in because if you send that to VCs like Lightspeed, I'm going to be like, wow, this is a really great company. I might not have met this if it wasn't for you. And now I'd love to lead the series A, and then we can put $20 million behind your investment on a much higher valuation. So, again, that's great for you guys. MICHAEL CARNEY: Yeah. NICOLE QUINN: And so, yeah, make sure to send that newsletter out. Maybe go to conferences, meet people that way, network. But, yeah, great question. MICHAEL CARNEY: Such great advice to end on and so on. Like I said, I wish we had more time because there's so much great knowledge and just experiences you've shared today with this community, Nicole. Before we hop off, I do have a quote that I've heard you speak to that I follow and almost-- might as well have on kind of my wall of inspiration-- and for anyone who wants to see, it's on Nicole's LinkedIn, the top of your profile as well. So "we have two ears and one mouth so that we can listen twice as much as we speak." And any last words there, Nicole, on just what that quote means to you and how you use that in your life today? NICOLE QUINN: That quote is very ironic given I just spoke for the last 48 minutes. MICHAEL CARNEY: It's perfect. It's perfect. NICOLE QUINN: But honestly, I never speak like this, right? So usually, my entire day looks like 20 different meetings, 20 half-an-hour meetings, longer for board meetings. And I sit there and just try to really ask more deep, philosophical questions to better understand who that founder is. And I hope I'm never talking more than 5% of the time because I think you learn so much more from what you listen to and truly hear. There's a difference between just listening and then really hearing what someone's saying. It's sort of reading between the lines. And so I like to live my life hearing what people are saying far more than talking. MICHAEL CARNEY: Well, we had to flip it today because you are our guest. But it's great words to live by. And, Nicole, we just want to thank you so much for joining today's session and just speaking on such amazing topics and such important subjects for us on the Google side and just for our listeners. So thank you so much for joining. NICOLE QUINN: Thank you so much. Thanks, Michael. Bye. MICHAEL CARNEY: Thanks, Nicole. Thank you, everyone, for joining today's talk with us on the Google side, and, again, a very big thank-you and shoutout to Nicole for hopping on for today and sharing such amazing words of wisdom. So awesome, everyone. We'll take care. [MUSIC PLAYING]
